doc.title: Leslie Gourse interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 9, 1996

title: Gourse's path to becoming a writer
summary: She wanted to write from her teens, studied playwriting at Columbia, turned to nonfiction, and credits her book-loving father and Shakespeare-quoting mother.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Was there experiences that you had in middle or high school that led you to being a writer and would you have any advice for aspiring writers these days?

I knew in my teens that I wanted to be a writer, early in my teens, and I wrote poetry to express whatever was going on in my mind, certain cares I had. And I excelled in that. I was good at it. And I went to college. I started as a playwriting major. I wanted to major in writing, but there were no courses really. I think that Columbia University and maybe Stanford on the west coast — is it Stanford? — no—

Well it’s a big school out there, I think it’s Stanford University, and there was a school in the Midwest, either Earlham or Morrison. There were very few schools that would let you major in writing when I started college which was 1956. So I went into the School of Dramatic Arts as a playwriting major at Columbia at the age of 17, and you know I didn’t know how to write. I was good at dialogue although it didn’t really show up at that time. And I switched into the school of general studies during the semester I was twenty, I turned twenty. I’d already been studying and I already knew that’s what I was going to go into, prose, and I wrote a novel. And from there I took one journalism course and didn’t get much out of that, but when I got out of school I wanted to go into non-fiction. Because that was the time when people were turning away from fiction to non-fiction. That’s when I think around that time Truman Capote wrote his non-fiction novel, or he was going to write it. It was in the air that non-fiction was going to reign and going to become regarded as high art. And I wanted — people wanted to deal with what was real, rather than — and it was hard to write fiction too, so I thought it was easier to write non- fiction, and it is, for me. So that’s how it happened. But I always knew — my father collected books, and my mother was always quoting Shakespeare. And we had good music in the house. We had jazz, we had classical, we had everything, so I had a good background in the arts and I was really led that way, influenced that was to become an artistic type. I could paint. If I weren’t a writer I’d probably be a portrait painter.
Well it was a good match then to put together your love of writing with your love of jazz and you’ve got quite a nice list of things you’ve done.
Yes I’ve done a lot. As I look back I say really, that’s a lot. I’m going to write another novel and maybe some screenplays. I’d like to do some screenplays.
